abstract: Temporal interference (TI) stimulation aims to engage deep brain structures noninvasively by superimposing two slightly detuned high-frequency electric fields (e.g. > 2 kHz), producing a low-frequency envelope (1-120 Hz) where they overlap. Existing accounts explain why a neuron responds to the envelope, but none identifies what determines which beat frequency a given neuron amplifies most. We address this using morphologically detailed, conductance-based models of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons and four interneuron subtypes, varying carrier frequency, envelope frequency, field amplitude, and orientation. Since the applied field contains no spectral component at the beat frequency, that response must first be generated by nonlinear membrane dynamics; we characterize the frequency-dependent gain applied to it once generated. That gain is band-pass: slow voltage-gated currents suppress the response at low frequencies and produce a peak at the resonant frequency. Modulated stimulation therefore outperforms an unmodulated carrier only when the envelope frequency matches the resonance of the relevant compartment, near its firing threshold. Notably, this advantage extends to carriers as low as 250 Hz, well below the minimum reported for simplified neuron models (1400-1700 Hz). Under distributed synaptic drive the advantage is lost, although frequency selectivity persists. Selectivity also varies across targets: because resonance depends on conductance composition, the optimal envelope frequency differs across compartments and cell types, and augmenting resonant conductances in parvalbumin-positive basket cells confers an advantage they otherwise lack. Carrier frequency is therefore less constrained than commonly assumed, and envelope frequency should be matched to the resonant properties of the target neuron type.
